Photograph: Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images US-Mexico border Rise in migrant deaths as 19 bodies found along Arizona border last month Pima county figures show highest number of monthly migrant deaths in two years as critics condemn US policy Tyler Hicks Fri 21 Aug 2026 08.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 08.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google According to newly released data from the medical examiner’s office in Pima county, Arizona , the remains of 19 migrants, including children, were recovered along the Arizona-Mexico border last month. The figure accounts for the highest number of monthly deaths in that area since 2024 and brings the number of total remains found to 73 this year, 14 more than the same time period last year. Experts and immigration advocates say the new data is a reflection of US policy abroad and at home, including the recent blocking of asylum seekers. Despite extreme temperatures caused by global warming and the threat of arrest by ICE , people are still making the perilous journey through Mexico. The US tried to stop cartel money-laundering. It devastated mom-and-pop businesses instead Read more “When the current administration is talking about closing the border, I think that they’ve been very effective at closing legal ports of entry and making it darn near impossible for people to actually enter the country or, as certain groups in the country like to say, ‘Come in the right way,’” said Octavio Torres, executive director of the non-profit Humane Borders organization. The group helps rescue migrants from dehydration and exposure and works alongside Pima county to track migrant deaths. Their data shows that at least 4,505 migrants have died in the Arizona desert over the last 25 years, an average of roughly one every other day. The most frequent causes of death are dehydration and exposure, but people also die from hypothermia or blunt force trauma caused by passing out and hitting their head on a rock. Brad Jones, a Humane Borders board member and professor with the Global Migration Center at the University of California, Davis, said the most recent data reveals a high number of “contemporaneous” deaths compared with recent years. This means the deaths occurred recently rather than representing old remains finally being discovered. Jones added that it’s often “random happenstance” when someone – a hiker or law enforcement officer, for instance – comes across human remains. The desert can quickly obscure or destroy evidence, and Jones said remains can “disappear without a trace pretty quickly” because of scavengers and animals. That means the true number of migrant deaths along the southern US border is undoubtedly higher than what’s known. “There’s estimates that the true number of migrant deaths ranges as high as four times what we’ve seen,” said Jones. “For every migrant’s remains that you find, how many do you not find?” Amelia Frank-Vitale, an anthropology professor at Princeton University, focuses on what compels people to risk death migrating to the US through harsh terrain like a desert or the Darién Gap, the dense jungle that connects Colombia and Panama. Oftentimes, she says, the people making these journeys feel like they have no choice at all. While researching and writing her book Leave If You Can: Migration and Violence in Bordered Worlds, Frank-Vitale traveled to Honduras and met a woman who was preparing to migrate while pregnant. “This is in the full throes of the Trump administration’s real attacks on immigrants,” Frank-Vitale said. “The actions of ICE are making international news. And still, she thought the best thing for her at this moment is maybe to try and get to the United States.” Frank-Vitale argues that the US has never fully addressed the role it’s played in creating instability in other countries whose people are now seeking refuge. But even before the Trump administration largely shuttered the asylum process, only a fraction of people from Central America – or, for that matter, from many parts of the world – were granted asylum. Torres, the executive director of Humane Borders, shares Frank-Vitale’s frustration with US policies that sow chaos then effectively neglect the people affected by that chaos. “Ever since Operation Gatekeeper in 1994 under the Clinton administration, it’s all been about prevention through deterrence,” Torres said, referring to a border patrol enforcement strategy that made crossing in safer, more obvious places extremely difficult. “Out of desperation, people think, ‘How else can I get in?’” Torres said. “And that’s what has driven people into the Arizona desert for the last 32 years.” The Trump administration turned the CBP One app from a digital appointment-maker to a means of encouraging “self-deportation”, and the administration also revived policies that require many asylum seekers to remain in Mexico while their cases proceed. As a result, the number of border “encounters” – a data point signifying when law enforcement encounters people at or between ports of entry – have plummeted since the Biden administration. But people are still coming, experts say; the journey is just harder and more lethal. Jones, the professor from California, compares the resulting deaths to a plane crash. “Suppose that every single July for 26 years straight, a Boeing 737 with between 100 and 250 passengers crashed right in the Arizona desert,” he said. “We’d be up in arms. You’d be freaking out.” One difference, he allows, is that deaths in the desert come in “dribs and drabs”. “But when you accumulate them,” he said, “we’re talking large numbers of deaths in any given year.” Explore more on these topics US-Mexico border Arizona US immigration news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

Photograph: ullstein bild/Getty Images From the Guardian archive Hungary Soviet troops invade Hungary – archive, 1956 On 4 November 1956, Russian forces moved into Budapest as part of an offensive against a national uprising that called for democratic reforms and an end to Soviet occupation Compiled by Richard Nelsson Wed 28 Oct 2026 09.09 EDT Last modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 09.47 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Soviet tanks crush resistance 5 November 1956 Before dawn yesterday Soviet armoured forces moved into Budapest and attacked “rebel” strongholds. At 8am the Soviet High Command in Hungary ordered Imre Nagy’ s government to surrender by noon “or Budapest will be bombed”. Soviet armoured forces then went into action. Just after 1pm Moscow radio announced: “The Hungarian counter-revolution has been crushed.” A mid-afternoon Moscow radio bulletin said that negligible groups of insurgents were offering resistance in Budapest but were being crushed. The radio also announced that a new “Revolutionary Workers’ and Peasants’ Government” had been formed under János Kádár, the former “Titoist” who became first secretary of the Communist party at one point in the rebellion. The Hungarian revolution begins – archive, October 1956 Read more Budapest radio had gone off the air at 8.10am with a woman’s appeal to “help Hungary … help, help, help …” In mid-afternoon a Vienna monitor picked up what was apparently the last rebel-held radio station in Hungary. It broadcast repeated calls for help. Civilised people of the world. On the watch tower of 1,000-year-old Hungary the last flames begin to go out. Soviet tanks and guns are roaring over Hungarian soil. Our women – mothers and daughters – are sitting in dread. They still have terrible memories of the army’s entry in 1945. Save our souls. This word may be the last from the last Hungarian freedom station. Listen to our call. Help us – not with advice, not with words, but with action, with soldiers and arms. The last news from Budapest itself reached the British Foreign Office in mid-afternoon. This said that Soviet troops were in control of key points and bridges in the city, although gunfire was still in progress. Other reports said that Mr Nagy, who attempted to restore democracy in the country after the insurrection, was under arrest, together with members of his government. Mr Nagy – now arrested – had given news of the Soviet attack to the world in a dramatic broadcast over Budapest radio. He spoke in English and then repeated his message in Hungarian. “This is Imre Nagy speaking,” he said. “In the early hours of this morning, Soviet troops started to attack the Hungarian capital with the apparent purpose of overthrowing the democratic government of the Hungarian People’s Republic.” After broadcasting frequent appeals to Russian troops not to fire on peaceful citizens, the radio then went off the air. Eisenhower appeals to Bulganin Mr Nagy, before he disappeared, had appealed through the British Legation for immediate intervention by the United Nations. Russia vetoed discussion of Hungary in the Security Council but the General Assembly, where the veto does not rule, voted overwhelmingly for an American resolution calling on the Soviet Union to halt its armed attack on Hungary and withdraw all its forces “without delay.” President Dwight D Eisenhower sent an urgent message to Marshal Bulganin , the Soviet Premier, asking him to withdraw the Soviet troops. The president expressed “shock and dismay” at the Soviet attack on the Hungarian people and urged that Hungary be given the right to choose its own government. The last minutes of freedom: panic as the Russian tanks arrive By Peter Howard 5 November 1956 Sopron, 4 November In this small town, the most westerly in Hungary, the last minutes of the revolution ran out to the rattle of machine-gun fire, the rumble of Soviet tanks, the screams and tears of women, and the singing of the Hungarian national anthem. Until 3pm, no Russian troops had entered Sopron, but they were known to be all around it, in the hills and woods. I arrived at Klingenbach, the nearest point in Austria, at three o’clock and decided to go in and have a look for myself. Approaching the Klingenbach I saw streams of Hungarian refugees, walking in little groups along the road, carrying their worldly belongings on their backs, or on oxcarts, handcarts or bicycles. Editorial: To quell the flames 5 November 1956 skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion Political turmoil and street protests: rebellion’s bitter legacy lives on Read more The “ forest fire, ” as the prime minister calls it, has not been put out. The flames are rising – and not only in the Middle East. They have spread to eastern Europe. For months or years to come it will be a matter of debate whether Britain’s attack on Egypt sparked Russia’s attack on Hungary. To say the least however, it is possible that British aggression tipped the scales in Soviet planning towards violent action: and British defiance of Assembly resolutions has sapped the strength of the United Nations at a most critical moment. Where Britain has rejected the Assembly’s wishes, Russia (though her crime may be greater) can follow. For the present, Hungary is doomed. For Hungary and eastern Europe there is tragically little that can be done. Russia can be condemned in the United Nations, but after the past week’s events that will mean little. It remains to be seen whether Russia is turning back entirely to a Stalinist line in foreign policy. Certainly the bankruptcy of its ideology has been displayed to the world in Hungary. If brute force is to be its method in future, we must expect mounting tension also between east and west in Europe. This is an edited extract. Read in full . Photograph: Intercontinental/AFP/Getty Images Belgrade sees reactionaries among the rebels 5 November 1956 Throughout the western countries governments and peoples yesterday protested against the Russians’ suppression of the Hungarian revolt. Even in Poland, still a communist country, a party leader expressed sympathy with the Hungarians. The official Yugoslav reaction was equivocal. The official news agency, Tanjug, said the use of foreign troops to clear up the internal affairs of a nation was contrary to the principles of Yugoslavia’s foreign policy, “but we cannot avoid the fact that the use of those troops was the result of a negative development in Hungary. Yugoslavs have with great concern followed the strong tendencies of reactionary elements, especially in Budapest – with murders of innocent people, the setting fire to books, and slogans which were smelling of the return to the Horthy era .” Moscow Radio accused Britain and France of raising the Hungarian question in the United Nations as a “smokescreen for the Anglo-French aggression in the Suez canal zone.” The broadcast went on: “Representatives of certain western powers should be the last ones to pose as defenders of the Hungarian people. It was precisely the long subversive activity of the imperialist powers that inspired and directed the actions of the reactionary forces in Budapest.” Paris : The French foreign minister, M Pineau, said France regretted that the United Nations had preferred to talk about Egypt rather than support the valiant Hungarian people. Berlin : The West Berlin radio stations played solemn music in contrast to their usually light Sunday programme. The communist radio of East Berlin continued its normal programme, including dance music. The East German Radio said it had received numerous telephone calls from workers offering help for Hungary or suggesting the creation of an “international brigade to assist the Hungarian workers in the struggle for freedom.” Copenhagen : About a thousand Danish students demonstrated outside the Russian embassy.
